Hi OP,

Don't stress too much about the PSI. You can go over or under.

If you go over and overinflate your tyres - they can blow up - but they will also have less rolling resistance, which means they take less energy from the motor to turn them - which means better fuel economy..

The down side to this is that you have less tyre contact with the road, which means you can't brake, corner or accelerate as well because the tyres become thinner.

If you under inflate you get the opposite - more rolling resistance which results in worse fuel economy, but better cornering, braking and acceleration (in simple terms. There's more to it than just this).

Do note though that the tyre can roll off the rim when its really low.

Also note that as you drive, the air in the tyres will heat up and expand - which will in turn increase the tyre pressure. So we have cold air which is denser and will produce a lower tyre psi, and hot air which will do the opposite.

I generally run somewhere between 30-40 psi. This will vary depending on which car, how heavy the load, my driving style.

When I am driving on the beach in a 4wd, or through the snow I will run around 10 psi (about 0.8 Bar or so).

When I'm wanting to slide the car around with little effort - I'll run around 40-50(50 is pretty high).

But to answer your question: don't be concerned. It will just drive a little funny and the steering will feel weird.

At 40 psi you'll experience a firmer ride, slightly more wear in the center of the tread, and less traction for winter driving. Especially around turns.

It's not an emergency but should be soon rectified. Simply press the valve stem and allow some air to escape. Most pressure guages have a nipple to assist here. Constantly remeasure as you do so. Bring the psi back to 34 or 32.

Ideally you'll do this immediately after driving a few miles,

I know I'm a bit late, but I just wanted to let you know that most decent car tires have a "max inflation" around 50 psi. Even lower end tires have a max inflation of around 44 psi.

Max inflation is found on the sidewall of the tire. This is the maximum "safe" pressure of the tire. A stationary tire will explode around 200 psi, depending on quality and tire condition. Add in driving conditions and this number will be lower, but no where near 40 psi for any tire.

As for wear pattern, over inflation will wear the center of the tire faster than the outside. I like to add +2 psi to my car tires to make them wear more evenly with my "driving type."

Pro Mechanic here. Allow me to elaborate.

The sticker in the car's door jamb (Lists tire pressure and size) is a recommendation used by the manufacturer that results in optimal fuel economy, and ride.

Now for the cons of over/under inflation.

An over inflated tire can have high spots, Which leads to uneven wear of the tires tread. This isn't much of a bad thing unless you don't have much tread on the tire as is.

An under inflated tire isn't necessarily bad, but a severely under inflated tire can damage the tire. My car's pressure for cold is 32psi. In the winter I lower it to 28psi as it increases traction for when driving on snow. It also works well for driving in the rain.

Driving a car with at least 1 tire that is over inflated can cause uneven wear. So I would suggest lowering the pressure so that the tires are all at even pressure (or close to it).
